definition.text: A well-drained, fertile type of soil found mainly in humid temperate climates.

facts.text: Brown earths lie mostly between 35° and 55° north, with the largest expanses in western and central Europe, Russia, eastern North America and eastern Asia; they cover 45% of England and Wales.
They form where rainfall is moderate, usually below 76 cm a year, and have a pH between 5.0 and 6.5.
The brownish A horizon, over 20 cm deep, is mull humus mixed into mineral matter by soil organisms and roots, so its boundary with the B horizon can be blurred.
The lighter B horizon is weathered parent material, often weakly illuviated; limited leaching moves only the more soluble bases down the profile.
Their rich colour comes from iron compounds, mainly complex oxides that are reddish-brown like rust, and the B horizon lacks the grey colours and mottles of gley soils.
Permeable and easy to work for most of the year, brown earths are valued for farming, and much of the deciduous woodland on them has been cleared.
The WRB calls the weakly leached brown earths Cambisols; German and Austrian taxonomy calls them Braunerde, and Polish classification maps them to Inceptisols in USDA Soil Taxonomy.
More strongly leached soils of continental eastern Europe, mapped as Luvisols, are called argillic brown earths in British and French systems for their clay-enriched horizon at depth.

definition.text: A class of the British soil classification, grouped with the podzolic soils but intermediate between podzols and brown earths.

facts.text: They form on hilly land in western Europe where more than about 900 mm of precipitation exceeds evapotranspiration for much of the year, so the profile is leached.
Their dark surface horizon holds more than 5% organic carbon, and unploughed examples may carry a mor humus layer.
Unlike true podzols they have no continuous E horizon: soil creeping downslope keeps supplying iron and aluminium oxides, which build up as a distinctive orange-brown B horizon.
The WRB calls them Umbrisols; they are common in Ireland, Scotland, Wales (about 20% of the country) and western England, and occur in the Appalachians.

definition.text: A shallow, humus-rich soil formed on carbonate-rich, or occasionally sulfate-rich, parent rock, recognized in British, German and some obsolete classifications.

facts.text: Limestone is by far the commonest parent rock, but rendzinas also form on dolomite, gypsum, marble, chalk and marl, typically on slopes in karst and mountain landscapes.
Water carrying dissolved carbon dioxide dissolves the carbonate and leaches it away, leaving the upper soil enriched in insoluble clay minerals.
Biological activity builds humus in the surface soil, where clay protects it from further decay; together clay and humus give dark colours and crumb structure.
Rendzinas in Wales have a simple A–C profile: dark calcareous topsoil directly over shattered limestone.
Typical pH is 5 to 8 with high base saturation; calcium and magnesium are plentiful but potassium is often low, so nutrient imbalances are common.
Rendzinas are a transitory stage: losing their carbonate turns them into another soil type, unless erosion keeps removing soil and holds them in place.
Shallowness hinders tillage and limits water storage, and slopes raise the erosion risk, so rendzina areas often keep semi-natural vegetation.
The WRB places rendzinas among Leptosols, Chernozems, Kastanozems or Phaeozems; the 1974 FAO world soil map called Leptosols on calcareous rock Rendzinas.

definition.text: A well-drained, reddish, clayey to silty soil of neutral pH, typical of the Mediterranean region.

facts.text: Its red colour comes from hematite forming in preference to goethite.
It covers limestone and dolomite bedrock in karst regions as a discontinuous layer from a few centimetres to several metres thick.
The karstic rock beneath gives it high internal drainage and neutral pH, surprisingly good drainage for a clay-rich soil.
Its drainage makes it popular for wine, in regions such as La Mancha in Spain and Coonawarra and the Barossa Valley in Australia.
As red Mediterranean soil, the class is formally superseded by systems such as the FAO's but still in common use, and as of 1997 it remained in Israel's and Italy's national classifications.
Its equivalents are chromic Luvisols on the UNESCO/FAO world map and rhodustalfs in USDA soil taxonomy.
Red Mediterranean soils developed fastest from the Miocene to the Late Pleistocene, during large climate fluctuations.
The 1938 USDA taxonomy described terra rossa as deep red soils of higher rainfall than rendzina.

title: Origin of terra rossa

definition.text: The long-running dispute among geologists, geomorphologists and soil scientists over what terra rossa formed from and how it relates to the carbonate rock beneath it.

facts.text: One group holds that terra rossa formed from the insoluble sediment and chert concentrated as the underlying carbonate rocks dissolved.
Another argues that residue alone cannot explain it: the soil is polygenetic, with parent material that includes volcanic ash, non-carbonate and wind-blown sediment depending on location.
A third group proposes that terra rossa formed by metasomatic replacement.

contested_note: Researchers disagree whether terra rossa is the insoluble residue of limestone, a polygenetic soil with exotic sediment, or a product of metasomatic replacement.

definition.text: A very dark, fertile, human-made soil (an anthrosol) of the Amazon Basin, also called Amazonian dark earth.

facts.text: Its black colour comes from weathered charcoal; it was made by adding charcoal, bones, broken pottery, compost and manure to poor Amazonian soil.
The charcoal from slash-and-char farming stays in the soil for thousands of years, binding minerals and nutrients, so terra preta resists leaching.
Pre-Columbian farming communities created it between 450 BCE and 950 CE; it can reach 2 m deep and is reported to regenerate at 1 cm a year.
It is surrounded by infertile terra comum, mainly Acrisols, Ferralsols and Arenosols; cleared Amazon soils lose their nutrients to rain or flooding within a short time.
The WRB calls it Pretic Anthrosol; most terra preta began as Ferralsol, and its A horizon holds more than 13–14% organic matter.
Estimates of its extent run from 0.1–0.3% of low forested Amazonia, or 6,300 to 18,900 square kilometres, to 10% or more; plots average 20 hectares.
It holds on average three times the organic matter of surrounding soils, up to 150 g/kg, and phosphorus reaches 200–400 mg/kg.
Lighter, brownish terra mulata, the farmed land around settlements, is more fertile than surrounding soils but less fertile than terra preta.

conflicts.text: Model-based predictions put terra preta at 3.2% of the forest.
conflicts.note: A third estimate of the same extent, between the 0.1–0.3% and 10% figures.

verification.title: Abundant and Stable Char Residues in Soils: Implications for Soil Fertility and Carbon Sequestration
verification.evidence: (Mollisols) contain char (generated by presettlement fires) that is structurally comparable to char in the Terra Preta soils and much more abundant than previously thought (~40-50% of organic C).
verification.note: the paper's 40-50% is char's share of organic carbon in Mollisols; the entry gives terra preta's extent and organic matter content

image.caption: Holger Casselmann, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

definition.text: The low-temperature charcoal, a form of pyrogenic or black carbon, that indigenous farmers added to poor soils to make terra preta.

facts.text: Some terra preta holds up to 9% black carbon against 0.5% in surrounding soils, and other measurements found carbon 70 times higher than in nearby Ferralsols.
Poly-condensed aromatic groups keep the charcoal stable against microbial breakdown for thousands of years.
Slow oxidation of the charcoal creates carboxylic groups that raise the soil's cation exchange capacity.
Its porous structure retains organic matter, water and dissolved nutrients, as well as pollutants such as pesticides.
Fresh charcoal must first be charged with nutrients, for example by soaking two to four weeks in a liquid nutrient, or it briefly depletes available nutrients.
Low-temperature charcoal carries an inner layer of condensates that bacteria consume; charring at high temperature burns it off and adds little fertility.
The earthworm Pontoscolex corethrurus eats charcoal and mixes it, finely ground, into the mineral soil.

title: Origin of terra preta

definition.text: The question of how Amazonian dark earths came to exist: made on purpose, built up from settlement refuse, or improved from naturally fertile patches.

facts.text: Early theories traced them to ashfall from Andean volcanoes or to sedimentation in ancient lakes or ponds.
Charcoal- and pottery-rich soil builds up by accident near dwellings, and many terra preta soils are now thought to have formed under kitchen middens as well as being made deliberately.
Recent research suggests terra preta may be natural, with pre-Columbian people using and improving scattered patches of existing fertility.
Variation among the dark earths leaves unclear whether all were made on purpose or whether the lightest are by-products of habitation.

contested_note: Sources differ on whether terra preta was made deliberately, accumulated as refuse, or began as naturally fertile soil that people improved.

definition.text: A fertilizer made from materials meant to replicate those of terra preta, such as crushed clay, blood and bone meal, manure and biochar.

facts.text: Being particulate, it can move down the soil profile and add fertility and carbon to existing peds and aggregates.
Poor tropical soils can be enriched to terra preta nova by adding charcoal and condensed smoke.
It might sequester carbon while reversing declining soil fertility and desertification, but whether this works at large scale is unproven.
Terra preta sanitation pairs lactic-acid treatment in urine-diverting dry toilets with vermicomposting as an alternative sanitation option.

title: Dark earth

definition.text: A dark, organic-rich layer up to 1 m thick that, in geology and archaeology, marks long-lasting human settlement.

facts.text: Charcoal in its organic matter gives the dark colour, and it may hold fragments of pottery, tile, animal bone and other artefacts.
It is read as soil enriched with sooty remains of thatch from chimneyless houses and other waste, and in some areas it seems to add fertility.
Archaeologists first called London's dark earth 'black earth', renaming it to avoid confusion with chernozem, whose colour is traditionally attributed to humus rather than soot.
Soot was used on purpose: Hebridean farmers spread old thatch from black houses on their fields each spring, and Achill Island farmers spread the sods of smoke huts.
In England it covers many areas built up in the Roman period, especially Londinium, between deposits dated to the 2nd–5th centuries and the 9th century.
Archaeologists debate whether London's dark earth records Roman refuse disposal or gardening or formed only after abandonment; French findings tie it to a switch from stone to timber and straw.
For at least 700 years West African farmers have enriched rainforest soils around their towns with compost of kitchen, animal, farm and fire waste, making a signature dark earth.
In Sweden, dark earth covers 40 hectares at Uppåkra and 7 hectares at the Viking town of Birka.

contested_note: Archaeologists disagree whether London's dark earth reflects Roman-period refuse or gardening, a population decline, or deposits formed after the city was abandoned.

definition.text: A reddish, clay-rich soil that typically develops in warm, temperate and humid climates and makes up about 13% of Earth's soil.

facts.text: Thin, highly leached organic and organic-mineral layers rest on a red layer of alluvium; the soil usually comes from weathered ancient crystalline and metamorphic rock.
High iron content gives colours from reddish brown to reddish yellow; Ultisols, Alfisols and Oxisols count as red soil once they develop this colour.
No single composition defines red soils, and one type may be infertile in one region but nutrient-rich in another.
Heavy leaching leaves them acidic and low in water-holding capacity, nutrients and humus; nitrogen is often deficient, and phosphorus and potassium run short after repeated harvests.
Liming raises their pH so acid-intolerant crops can thrive, though it can stimulate microbes that deplete organic matter and harm soil structure.
Organic manure, suitable tillage and crop rotation raise their organic matter, fertility and water retention.
They make up much farmland in tropical, subtropical and Mediterranean zones: about 102 million hectares in China and about 350,000 km², 10.6% of the country, in India.
India's red soils, nicknamed the omnibus group, formed on Precambrian granites, gneisses and quartzites; they are thin and poor in the uplands but deep, fertile loams on the lower plains.

definition.text: A tropical rainforest soil, also called tropical red earth, with a relatively high content of iron and aluminium oxides.

facts.text: Latosols are usually classed as Oxisols in USDA soil taxonomy or Ferralsols in the WRB.
Red or yellowish-red throughout from iron oxides, they lack the distinct horizons of a podzol and often reach 20–30 m deep, against 1–2 m for podzols.
A thin but very fertile humus layer from the forest above overlies an infertile layer stripped by rapid leaching under high rainfall.
Fertility depends wholly on the rainforest: once it is felled and the humus is no longer replaced, the nutrients leach away quickly.

definition.text: An uncommon soil formed from weathered ultramafic rock, such as peridotite and serpentinite, that contains minerals of the serpentine group.

facts.text: Its minerals include antigorite, lizardite and chrysotile, or white asbestos; the ultramafic parent rocks contain more than 70% iron or magnesium minerals.
Steep, rocky, erosion-prone serpentine terrain keeps the soils shallow, and with sparse vegetation they run hot and dry.
Often reddish, brown or grey from high iron and little organic matter, it has a low calcium-to-magnesium ratio and little nitrogen, phosphorus or potassium.
It carries high concentrations of heavy metals, including chromium, iron, cobalt and nickel, and is generally poor for agriculture.
Serpentinite forms when olivine-rich peridotite reacts with water, mostly in oceanic crust near mid-ocean ridges; its chrysotile asbestos makes dust from crushed rock a health hazard.
Serpentine soils occur worldwide, partly mirroring ophiolites, from the Balkans, Cyprus and the Alps to Cuba and New Caledonia; most North American ones are in California.
Adding gypsum or other soluble calcium improves the calcium-to-magnesium ratio, so amended soils can support crops and pasture.
Plants adapted to its heavy metals have been used in phytoremediation to remove metals from polluted soil.

definition.text: The distinctive flora of serpentine soils, marked by poor productivity, high endemism and tolerance of drought, heavy metals and scarce nutrients.

facts.text: Plants often have a stunted habit and dull, waxy grey-green leaves that help retain water and reflect sunlight.
Low calcium-to-magnesium ratios limit root growth and nutrient uptake, and heavy metals stunt growth and cause chlorosis; plants respond with deep roots, metal exclusion or storage, and tolerance.
In California 45% of serpentine-associated taxa are rare or endangered, and 10% of the state's plants are serpentine endemics.
Serpentine tolerance has evolved many times, and patchy, isolated habitats limit gene flow while promoting speciation.

definition.text: Grassland or savanna on serpentine outcrops where the climate would otherwise support forest, found as an ecoregion in parts of the United States.

facts.text: Barrens are most likely where ultramafic rock never received richer sediment carried by water, glaciers or wind, such as loess, sand or volcanic ash.
They occur on altered ultramafic ophiolites in small, scattered areas of the Appalachians and the Coast Ranges of California, Oregon and Washington.
Grazing serpentine land carries metal risks: one study found toxic nickel in the kidneys of 20% of grazing animals and toxic copper in the livers of 32%.
Fire suppression turned Pennsylvania's Rock Springs barren from grassland to forest, while controlled burns since 1995 have restored sparse species at Buck Creek, North Carolina.

definition.text: An Australian term for a soil with a sharp contrast in texture between its horizons, also called a texture contrast soil.

facts.text: In Northcote's Factual Key, the B horizon is at least one and a half texture classes finer than the A horizon, with a clear to sharp change within 0.1 m.
Topsoils range from coarse sand to clay loam and subsoils from light to heavy clay; some have a bleached A2 horizon.
Northcote used colour to separate brown, red and yellow duplex soils; the Australian Soil Classification spreads them among Podosols, Sodosols, Chromosols and Kurosols.
Similar soils in strongly seasonal climates such as the Mediterranean are called calcic and chromic Luvisols.

definition.text: A non-alluvial, non-calcareous loamy or clayey soil with a dense, impervious subsurface horizon, classed among the gleyic soils.

facts.text: Continual waterlogging bleaches the topsoil; it often forms on sandy material over dense subsoil in cool, moist climates.
Nutrient-poor, often highly acidic and poorly aerated, it suits woodland such as English oak rather than crops.
Where saturated all year it becomes bog stagnogley and eventually bog, as in the missen of the Black Forest.
Related to the pseudogleys, stagnogleys occur in perhumid climates and on steep slopes, in Germany's Central Uplands and on the Midvale Ridge in the UK.

definition.text: A superficial deposit of homogeneous loam or silt, first named in southern England, that is periglacial wind-blown loess.

facts.text: It was laid down in the Pleistocene, when wind picked up fine sediment from glacial outwash in cold, dry periods and dropped it where the wind slackened.
It lies in discontinuous spreads up to a metre deep across southern England and South Wales, with commercial deposits about 2 to 4 m thick in Kent, Hertfordshire and Hampshire.
Its name comes from brick-making: it needs little or no added material to make stock bricks, which harden at lower temperatures than clay bricks.
It gives rich, fertile farmland, but it collapses rapidly when saturated and makes a poor foundation for buildings.

definition.text: A soil dominated by very fine clay particles, often with small amounts of sand or organic material.

facts.text: Gumbo holds water exceptionally well, but rain turns it into a sticky mud that is hard to work with large farm machinery.
No-till farming on gumbo appears strongly correlated with higher yields than traditional tillage.

definition.text: A smooth, bare clay flat in the deserts of Central Asia, similar to a salt flat; the Turkic name means 'smooth, even, or bare'.

facts.text: A takir forms in a shallow depression of heavy clay soil that floods after seasonal rains.
As the water evaporates, a dried, fissured crust forms on the surface, often colonised by filamentous cyanobacteria.
Similar flats are called playas or salt flats in the southwestern United States and sabkha in Arab countries.
Calcisols were formerly known internationally as Desert soils and Takyrs.

definition.text: Soil formed in sediment of shallow, permanently flooded environments, or in any area under water too deep for rooted plants to grow.

facts.text: Shallow-water sediments undergo soil-forming processes, can support rooted plants such as eelgrass, and meet Soil Taxonomy's definition of soil, opening a new frontier for soil survey.
Submerged soils formed on land and were later flooded by rising water tables, beaver dams or sea level rise; subaqueous soils formed under a continuous water column, as in an estuary.
Proposals to treat submersed sediments as soil date from the mid-1800s, but the US concept arose only in the early 1990s, pioneered by George Demas in Maryland's Chesapeake Bay.
Demas saw that these areas supported rooted plants and had formed horizons; later study showed additions, losses and transformations of energy and matter.
Soil survey inventories use an arbitrary water depth limit of 2.5 m, which some states have extended to 5 m.
Treating them as soils rather than sediments lets scientists study linked horizons across the underwater landscape, aiding management of shallow-water habitats and seagrass restoration.
Under submergence, as in rice fields, wetlands, estuaries and flood plains, nitrogen dynamics differ from those of aerated soils.

definition.text: Surveying underwater soils much as land soils are mapped, except that the mapper works from the water.

facts.text: Bathymetric maps take the place of topographic maps and aerial photographs for identifying underwater landscapes and landforms.
Augers with extendable shafts, peat corers and vibracores replace shovels for taking samples.
Several US states have begun mapping subaqueous soils, each NRCS state office setting its priority by local conservation concerns.
Interpretations for various uses are still being developed and are expected to grow as more areas are surveyed.

definition.text: An accumulation of partially decayed vegetation or organic matter, found in peatlands, bogs, mires, moors and muskegs.

facts.text: Sphagnum, or peat moss, is one of its commonest components, though many other plants contribute.
Peat forms in wetlands where flooding or stagnant water cuts off oxygen and slows decomposition; soils made mainly of peat are Histosols.
There are about 4 trillion cubic metres of peat in the world.
Peat stores up to 550 Gt of carbon, 42% of all soil carbon and more than all other vegetation including forests, while covering just 3% of the land surface.
Peat is renewable in principle, but it regrows only about 1 mm a year, and in only 30–40% of peatlands, far slower than industrial extraction.
Over geological time peat is often the first step toward coal, especially low-grade lignite.
Centuries of burning and draining peat have released much CO2, contributing to human-caused climate change.
Engineers treat highly organic peat soil as a problem: it consolidates poorly and makes an unstable foundation for roads or buildings.

conflicts.text: Joosten and Clarke say peatlands hold one third of the world's soil carbon.
conflicts.note: Differs from the 42% of all soil carbon given in the Peat lead.

conflicts.text: PEATMAP puts global peatland coverage at 4.23 million km², about 2.84% of the world land area.
conflicts.note: Differs slightly from the 3% of the land surface given with the carbon figure.

verification.evidence: Grassy.—Material contains more than 15 percent fibers that can be identified as grass, sedges, cattails, and other grasslike plants and contains more grassy fibers than any other kind of fiber (e.g., grassy mucky peat).
verification.note: the Manual's 15% is the fiber threshold for grassy peat material; the entry gives peat's share of soil carbon and regrowth

image.caption: David Stanley from Nanaimo, Canada, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

definition.text: The build-up of peat where plant material fails to decay fully under acidic, oxygen-poor, waterlogged conditions.

facts.text: Peat is made mainly of wetland vegetation, principally bog plants such as mosses, sedges and shrubs.
Accumulating peat holds water, slowly making conditions wetter so the wetland expands.
Sphagnum promotes its own habitat: it secretes tannins that preserve organic material, and its water-holding hyaline cells keep the bog constantly wet.
Most modern peat bogs formed 12,000 years ago at high latitudes, after the glaciers retreated at the end of the last ice age.
Peat usually accumulates at about a millimetre a year, so boreal peatlands take thousands of years to reach their average depth of 1.5 to 2.3 m.
Northern peatlands hold an estimated 415 gigatonnes of carbon, tropical peatlands 50 Gt and South American ones 15 Gt.

verification.title: Global peatland dynamics since the Last Glacial Maximum
verification.evidence: Tropical peatlands have accumulated 50 (44–55) GtC, with rapid rates about 8000–4000 years ago affected by a high and more stable sea level, a strong summer monsoon, and before the intensification of El Niño.
verification.note: the paper's 8000-4000 years ago is the period of rapid tropical peat accumulation; the entry gives when most high-latitude bogs formed (12,000 years ago)

definition.text: The division of peat material into fibric, hemic and sapric kinds by how far it has decomposed.

facts.text: Fibric peat is the least decomposed and consists of intact fibre; hemic peat is partly decomposed and sapric peat the most decomposed.
Phragmites peat, made of reed grass and other grasses, is denser than many other kinds of peat.

definition.text: The record of past vegetation, pollen, spores, animals and archaeological remains preserved layer by layer in a peat profile.

facts.text: Because peat builds up over thousands of years, preserved pollen and plant remains let scientists reconstruct past vegetation, climate and land use.
The peatland scientist Harry Godwin coined the phrase in 1981.
Peat records are compared with modern bogs to gauge human effects on the mercury cycle, dated with methods such as the vertical distribution of lead-210.
Acidic, tanning water and the antibiotic sphagnan preserve bog bodies almost perfectly, such as Denmark's Tollund Man, who lived in the 4th century BC.

title: Peat drainage

definition.text: The draining of peat soils, often through canals, for agriculture, forestry and peat extraction.

facts.text: Drainage exposes organic carbon, built up underwater over thousands of years, to the air, where it decomposes to CO2.
About 12% of current peatlands have been drained and damaged; as of 2022 they emit an estimated 4% of human-made greenhouse gases, not counting fires.
Draining peat also destroys the habitat of many species.
The Netherlands, largely peat 2,500 years ago, has lost peatland to drainage-driven compaction, oxidation and excavation, leaving about 2,733 km², 10% of its land.
England's peatlands store 584 million tonnes of carbon but emit around 11 million tonnes of CO2 a year through degradation and draining.

verification.note: the Manual's 15% is the fiber threshold for grassy peat material; the entry gives the share of peatland drained

title: Peat fires

definition.text: Fires in peat deposits, which smoulder underground for long periods and are not put out by light rain.

facts.text: Peat's high carbon content lets it burn when dry; once ignited, for example by a wildfire reaching below the surface, it smoulders.
Smouldering fires can creep undetected through underground peat for months, years or even centuries.
Bogs naturally burn and depend on wildfires to stop woody plants lowering the water table and shading out bog plants.
In 1997 peat and forest fires in Indonesia released between 0.81 and 2.57 gigatonnes of carbon, equal to 13–40% of carbon from global fossil fuel burning.
A 2010 heat wave of up to 40 °C ignited peat in Central Russia, and in June 2019 Arctic peat fires emitted 50 megatonnes of CO2.
Climate change makes peat fires much more likely than before.

notes: May overlap a soils-in-the-landscape entry drafted from the Peatland page; merge if so.

verification.evidence: Grassy.—Material contains more than 15 percent fibers that can be identified as grass, sedges, cattails, and other grasslike plants and contains more grassy fibers than any other kind of fiber (e.g., grassy mucky peat).
verification.note: the Manual's 15% is the fiber threshold for grassy peat material; the entry gives Indonesian fire carbon as a share of fossil emissions

definition.text: A form of erosion at the sides of gullies cut into peat, leaving overhanging banks of peat and vegetation.

facts.text: Hags form when flowing water cuts down into the peat or when fire or overgrazing exposes its surface.
Exposed peat then erodes further under wind, water and livestock.
Hags are too steep and unstable for plants to establish, so they keep eroding unless restored.

definition.text: Dried peat burned for heat and power, traditionally cut by hand and left to dry in the sun.

facts.text: In Ireland and Scotland peat was stacked to dry and used for cooking and home heating, a tradition traced back to the Roman period.
Ireland's state-owned Bord na Móna milled peat for power stations and sold peat briquettes for domestic heating.
In 1929 over 40% of the Soviet Union's electricity came from peat, falling to 1% by 1980.
Some Scotch whisky distilleries, such as those on Islay, dry malted barley over peat fires.

verification.evidence: Grassy.—Material contains more than 15 percent fibers that can be identified as grass, sedges, cattails, and other grasslike plants and contains more grassy fibers than any other kind of fiber (e.g., grassy mucky peat).
verification.note: the Manual's 15% is the fiber threshold for grassy peat material; the entry gives peat's share of Soviet electricity

definition.text: The use of peat as a raw material for gardening and horticulture, now being restricted in some places.

facts.text: Kew Gardens has discouraged peat as a soil additive since 2003, and the Royal Horticultural Society promotes peat-free gardening.
Bark- and coir-based peat-free potting mixes are rising in the UK, while peat is still used in other European countries, Canada and parts of the US.
In 1999 the UK set its horticulture industry a target of 90% peat-free by 2010; Chile has forbidden peat extraction since April 2024.
Peat grow cups have about 4.5 times the carbon footprint of single-use plastic cups.

verification.title: Open-source manufacturing of polypropylene replacements for peat cups in vertical farming: improvements in life cycle embodied energy, greenhouse gas emissions, labor and operational costs
verification.evidence: For relatively low-value kale, despite higher experimental yields the net profit advantage of peat cups was only 2.2 % over the agrivoltaic agrotunnel system lifetime.
verification.note: the paper compares peat cups with polypropylene cups (profit, energy, impacts); the entry gives the UK peat-free target

verification.evidence: Grassy.—Material contains more than 15 percent fibers that can be identified as grass, sedges, cattails, and other grasslike plants and contains more grassy fibers than any other kind of fiber (e.g., grassy mucky peat).
verification.note: the Manual's 15% is the fiber threshold for grassy peat material; the entry gives the UK peat-free target

title: Peatland restoration

definition.text: Repairing damaged peatlands, usually by blocking drainage channels so they rewet and native vegetation recovers.

facts.text: Rewetting limits carbon release in the short term, and new vegetation later supplies the litter that restarts peat formation.
Active reintroduction of peatland plants re-establishes typical communities within 5 years, supporting the return of animals, insects and birds.
Pools in restoration projects raise biodiversity by adding microhabitats.
The Convention on Biological Diversity names peatlands as key ecosystems to protect, and wetlands are also protected under the 1971 Ramsar Convention.

notes: May overlap a soils-in-the-landscape entry drafted from the Peatland page; merge if so.

definition.text: Permanently frozen peat ground, which makes up around half the area of northern peatlands.

facts.text: Permafrost peatlands are about a tenth of all permafrost area and hold about a tenth of permafrost carbon, 185 ± 66 Gt.
Dry peat insulates well, with a thermal conductivity of around 0.25 W m−1 K−1, shielding permafrost from thaw and forming palsas and peat plateaus.
Thaw tends to raise methane emissions while only slightly increasing CO2 uptake, adding to the permafrost carbon feedback.
Under 2 °C of global warming, 0.7 million km² of peatland permafrost could thaw.

title: Tropical peat

definition.text: A histosol of tropical latitudes, found in South East Asia, Africa and Central and South America.

facts.text: It forms mostly from dead trees rather than the sphagnum typical of temperate peat.
Its organic matter content usually exceeds 75%, with a low dry bulk density.
Tropical peatlands cover about 380,000 km², roughly 0.25% of Earth's land, yet hold 50,000–70,000 million tonnes of carbon, about 3% of global soil carbon.
About 46% of tropical peat area is in South America, though the world's largest tropical peatland is in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Peat swamp forests yield timber, bark, resins and latex and shelter endangered species such as the orangutan.
Once the forest is cleared and the peat drained, surface peat oxidises and loses carbon rapidly as CO2, and the sinking surface causes local flooding.
Plantations, logging and fire are shrinking the carbon store; Indonesia's burning peat bogs contain more than 50 billion tonnes of carbon.
Leaving these emissions out underestimates the rise in atmospheric greenhouse gases and human-induced climate change.

notes: S:9cc67945e6d5 gives the dry bulk density as 'around 0.2 mg/m3 (0.0 gr/cu ft)', apparently a unit error; the fact omits the number. May overlap a soils-in-the-landscape entry drafted from the Peatland page; merge if so.

definition.text: A soil of moderate inherent fertility, between eutrophic and oligotrophic soils.

facts.text: Base status, an indicator of fertility, relates the major nutrient cations (calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium) to the soil's clay percentage.
It is commonly expressed in hundredths of a mole of cations per kilogram of clay, cmol(+) kg−1 clay.

definition.text: A lightweight black carbon residue made by strongly heating wood or other plant and animal material in minimal oxygen, driving off water and volatile compounds.

facts.text: In traditional charcoal burning, a kiln or conical pile burns part of its own wood under limited oxygen to char the rest; modern retorts are more efficient.
Research on Amazonian terra preta revived charcoal's use in horticulture, both to improve soils and to sequester carbon.
Biochar is a form of charcoal, sometimes modified, intended for organic uses such as adding to soil.
Large-scale charcoal production has long driven deforestation, particularly in Central Europe.

definition.text: Earthy material used to fill a depression or hole, build mounds or otherwise artificially change the level of land.

facts.text: It is usually subsoil and underlying parent material, with little organic matter or biological activity, and may include sand, rocks and stones.
Fill should be as free of organic matter as possible, since decomposing organic matter leaves voids that make the fill settle and can damage structures on it.
Common uses are building up highway shoulders and raising low construction sites against flooding; Kansai International Airport stands on a new fill island of about five square kilometres.
Most fill is mined from commercial sand and gravel pits and must meet the gradation specifications set by the project's geotechnical engineer.

definition.text: Thick deposits of soft, water-saturated, unconsolidated silty clay on the floors of certain estuaries, mostly in temperate regions shaped by glacial cycles.

facts.text: With low shear strength, high compressibility and low permeability, and a typical bulk density of about 1.3 g/cm³, it is hazardous to build on in seismic areas such as San Francisco Bay.
It forms from alluvial clay, silt and sand washed in by tributary streams and, in glacial periods, from a separate layer of silt, sand and organic detritus.
Heavy buildings need deep foundations on stiffer layers below the mud, and even then the surrounding ground settles over time, damaging utility connections.
Exposed at low tide it forms mudflats, feeding grounds for shorebirds and a substrate for eelgrass, cordgrass and pickleweed.

definition.text: A grassland ecosystem on thin, basic soils such as those of chalk and limestone downland, also called alkaline grassland.

facts.text: Large areas occur in northwestern Europe, especially on Salisbury Plain and the North and South Downs of England; machair is a variant on calcium-rich shell sand.
Its plants are short, hardy grasses and herbs such as clover, held at a plagioclimax by sheep or cattle grazing.
It is an important habitat for insects, particularly butterflies and ants.
Its lichen communities, favoured by stable flints and nutrient-poor soil, have declined since the mid-20th century through reduced grazing, nitrogen deposition and habitat loss.

definition.text: A sticky, plastic, bluish-grey clay soil formed from highly weathered serpentinite mélange.

facts.text: Its colour comes from gleying under anaerobic conditions; a greyer variant is called grey goo.
It weathers from the Franciscan Complex, a mélange of greenstones, cherts, basalts, shales, sandstones, schists and serpentinites sheared between the Pacific and North American plates.
Its clay holds much water and drains poorly; saturated, it slips, especially in shallow soils under heavy rain, feeding landslides on the Northern California coast.
It has been found only in the Trinidad and Orick regions of Humboldt County, California.

title: Growstones

definition.text: A plant-growing substrate made from recycled glass, used without soil or as a soil conditioner.

facts.text: It has more air and water retention space than perlite and peat, and holds more water than parboiled rice hulls.
Growstones appear to be a comparable alternative to expanded clay aggregate.
The maker, Growstone, ceased operations on January 26, 2019.

notes: A single company's product, and the company ceased operations in 2019 (products are excluded unless they pass tests 1–2; it has its own article but is not a soil type). If kept, it belongs in Farming systems and growing media.

definition.text: The upper of the two layers of an undisturbed peat bog, holding living plants, which overlies the catotelm.

facts.text: Its lower boundary usually coincides with the lowest level of the water table, which fluctuates within it, so conditions swing between aerobic and anaerobic.
It has higher hydraulic conductivity and lower bulk density than the catotelm.
Ditching before peat harvesting thickens the acrotelm and dries the peat, while drainage and subsidence lower hydraulic conductivity.
A fully developed acrotelm, found only in ombrotrophic bogs, lets researchers study atmospheric deposition.

definition.text: A mixture of organic and mineral materials, often including repurposed organic waste, designed to approximate natural soil and grow plants.

facts.text: Constructed soils reclaim degraded land without usable topsoil, such as mines, landfills and industrial or urban sites, and are classed as Technosols.
They are preferred to imported topsoil, since harvesting topsoil degrades a second site and usually costs more.
Layers thinner than about 45 cm tend to be uniform topsoil mixes; thicker ones can mimic natural horizons, using cheaper material for subsoil and a sand or gravel drainage layer.
Abrupt changes in texture and bulk density between layers govern lateral versus vertical water flow and perched water.
They combine a mineral fraction that sets texture, an organic fraction supplying nutrients and a slowly decomposing carbon source such as wood chips or biochar.
Topsoil organic matter should not exceed 15% by weight, or the soil settles and waterlogs, and a C:N near 20:1 gives a sustained release of nutrients.
They usually omit living organisms and lack stable structure, relying on biotic processes and pedogenesis to start as the site revegetates.
They must meet regulatory limits for pathogens, harmful trace elements, salinity and pH.

definition.text: A fertile, low-lying grassy plain of dune grassland on parts of the north-western coasts of Ireland and Scotland, especially the Outer Hebrides.

facts.text: It forms from shell fragments rolled ashore by waves, broken up and blown inland, a theory first put forward by William MacGillivray in 1830.
Machair is highly calcareous, with 20% to 80% calcium carbonate on the beaches, and its pH is typically above 7.
The sandy soil holds nutrients poorly and lacks copper, cobalt and manganese, so cattle need supplements and only some oats, rye and bere barley thrive.
Seaweed spread by early farmers protected and fed the soil, and buried kelp composts into fertile beds.

title: Black cotton soil
article: Major soil deposits of India#Black soils

definition.text: The black, clayey soil of India's Deccan Plateau, also called regur, named for its suitability for growing cotton.

facts.text: It forms from Deccan trap lava flows and covers about 300,000 square kilometres of the north-western Deccan Plateau.
Rich in montmorillonite clay, it retains water well and holds calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash and lime.
In hot, dry spells it cracks, which aerates the soil; it is very hard when dry and muddy when wet, needing deep tillage for drainage.
Engineers find it highly compressible, with low bearing capacity and low shear strength.

notes: Chernozem's lead (S:5221fb0e4451) also lists regur and black cotton soil as names for chernozem.

definition.text: The soil of flooded rice paddies, counted among the anthropogenic soils.

facts.text: Methanogens thrive in rice paddy soil, where methane forms from the anaerobic decomposition of organic matter in the flooded field.
Methanogenesis occurs even though paddy soil is temporarily oxygenated.
PLFA analysis found paddy soil's bacteria–archaea community about 44% aerobic bacteria, 32% facultative anaerobes and 24% archaea.
The smectite-rich paddy soils of Thailand's Central Plains are among the most productive in the world.
